summary: An informational memo to focus discussion on problems of running out of top-level domain names and conflicts when many organizations want the same name. It proposes a convention for using legal names as domain names.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2352 proposes a way of naming companies on the Internet that follows the law of the country they are in. Instead of competing for the same name under a generic domain, an organisation would get a name under its own country code, derived from the legal name it already has registered. The idea is that whoever holds the legal name holds the domain name, so the disputes stop.

subtitle: A proposal to hang company and trademark names under country domains so the law, not the registry, settles who owns a name.

tldr.problem: The generic domain space runs out of desirable names, and organisations that both have a legitimate claim to the same name end up in costly legal disputes that the domain name registries have no way to settle.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes a functional hierarchy under each country code domain, built from the identifiers that country already uses for companies and trademarks, so the name registry follows the local register of legal names rather than inventing its own.
tldr.outcome: The document is an independent submission rather than a working group product, and the RFC Editor's note records that it appeared to depend on corporations changing their domain names without any incentive, and that it may not be politically feasible to implement as described.

today: RFC 2352 is an Informational memo published in May 1998, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It is an independent submission rather than a working group document, and the RFC Editor's note records that it appeared to depend on corporations changing their domain names from their present form to more cumbersome handles without any incentive, and that it may not be politically feasible to implement as described.

sections.title: The Problem: Exhaustion and Conflicts
sections.content:
The memo exists to focus discussion on two problems: the exhaustion of the top level domain space, and the conflicts that can occur when multiple organisations are vying for the same name. The solutions it proposes are meant as a framework for development, so that a general consensus emerges about the appropriate answer in each case, leading eventually to the adoption of standards.

The domain space is a hierarchical tree-structured namespace with several top level domains and sub-domains beneath them. The TLDs are split into generic top-level domains, the gTLDs, and two-letter ISO 3166 country domains for every country in which Internet connectivity is provided. The allocation of sub-domains under a TLD is entirely up to the registry for that TLD, which may create further levels of structure or merely allocate domains in a flat manner.

The three examples in the memo show what that means. Under a gTLD the allocation is inherently flat, because organisations are allocated domain names directly under the TLD, so a name such as VAUGHAN.COM tells you the organisation is commercial but not what country it is based in. Under a country domain the policy can vary widely from country to country: some mirror the gTLD structure, some use a geographical structure, some have no sub-structure at all. A flat country domain such as AXA.SOL.FR tells you the organisation is based in France but, without studying the actual organisation name, not what type it is. A hierarchical country domain such as AC.NEWPORT.UK tells you the country, and by following the hierarchy, that the organisation is academic. While the system is flexible in not enforcing a strict hierarchy, that flexibility can lead to exhaustion of domain names in the generic space and to conflicts between organisations who may both have a legitimate claim to a particular name.
sections.plainLanguage: The name space is a tree, and each registry decides how to fill in its own branch. Some fill it flat, some in layers. The flat generic branches fill up, and then two firms that both have a right to the same word end up arguing about it.

sections.title: Why Not More Generic Top-Level Domains
sections.content:
One proposed solution to name exhaustion is to create more gTLDs, so that organisations with the same name can be registered uniquely under different TLDs, with names such as FIRM, STORE, WEB, ARTS, REC, INFO and NOM. The memo lists three disadvantages. It creates confusion in users' minds as to what TLD refers to a particular organisation: MCDONALDS.COM might be the fast food corporation and MCDONALDS.FIRM a firm of lawyers, and the user has no way of telling which is which. To prevent that confusion, big corporations will simply reserve all the variations of the name, IBM.COM, IBM.FIRM, IBM.STORE and so on, so the name exhaustion and conflict problems are not solved but made worse. And the names of legitimate trade mark holders can still be acquired by anybody, which leads to potential conflicts.

Another set of possible solutions, discussed by the World Intellectual Property Organisation, addresses only dispute resolution when trademarks are used as domain names under gTLDs, and not the full legal context of their origin of registration.
sections.plainLanguage: The obvious fix, more generic endings such as .firm or .store, makes things worse. People cannot tell which ending means what, large firms grab every variant of their own name, and anyone can still take a name that belongs to a trade mark holder.

sections.title: The Proposal: Legal Names Under Country Domains
sections.content:
The memo argues that, with the domain name system hierarchical, it would seem a good idea to expand on the existing structure rather than create several duplicate structures, and that it is not a good idea to create new gTLDs which merely overlap the existing ones.

The proposal allows for country-code based domain names related to legally registered names in the country, or locality, state or province, that they are based in, by creating a functional hierarchy beneath the country TLD. It does not seek to do away with gTLDs, but suggests that a legal name should be sought first and then, if desired, a generic name used alongside it, so that in case of any dispute the organisation has a legally-held name which no other organisation could claim.

The argument behind it is that the world is not flat: with the expansion of the Internet to a truly global medium, the notion that there can only be one commercial entity, one organisation and one network provider with the same name seems impossible, and the present system finds itself in that position, with a constantly spiralling number of disputes over who owns or deserves a certain name and an increasing number ending in unnecessary and costly legal action. Two advantages follow. Deciding what names belong to which organisation is no longer a function of the domain name registry but of the company name or trade mark registration authority in the given locality, so disputes over names cannot arise, since all names are unique within the context of the legal name. And because all names are unique, there should be no exhaustion, deliberate or otherwise, of desirable names by other concerns, as all the owners of legally-held names automatically have the right to the relevant domain name.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposal is to hang names under the country code of the country the organisation is in, using the words that country already uses to register company names and trade marks. Whoever holds the legal name then holds the domain name, and no one else can claim it.

sections.title: How a Legal Sub-Domain Is Written
sections.content:
The sub-domain identifiers are created from the existing identifiers for company names and trade marks within the given locality, state, province or country. The general form is a legal token, then locality identifiers, then the ISO 3166 country code. The examples are LTD.UK for limited companies in the UK, PLC.UK for public limited companies in the UK, TM.FR for trademarks in France, INC, LTD, CO or CORP followed by a state and US for incorporated bodies in the United States, LLC followed by a state and US for limited liability companies, and GMBH.DE for German companies.

The registry for the appropriate upper level country, state, province or locality domain creates the entries in these sub-domains based on the laws for allocating such legal names in that particular country, state, province or locality. The full legal name is used, but omitting the legal token such as Ltd or Corp, since that is determined by the choice of upper level domain. All spaces within the name are converted to hyphens, and other punctuation is either disregarded or also converted into hyphens. For holders of international trademarks and other international names, the gTLD INT can be used in place of the country identifier, as in TM.INT or REG.INT.

In countries that do not have existing sub-structure, the memo strongly recommends creating other sub-domains as well, for commercial entities, organisations and academic entities, to reduce the remaining conflicts from organisations that are not legally registered. The representation of any domain element is limited to the ASCII character set of alphabetic characters, digits and the hyphen, as described in RFC 1035, so names in languages that use other character sets are limited by that definition. The registration of non-textual trade marks such as logos or three dimensional shapes is beyond the scope of the document; the memo judges it unlikely that such marks will need to be used the way domain names are used presently, but does not explicitly prohibit them.
sections.plainLanguage: The name is written in three parts: what kind of body it is, the place inside the country, and the country code. The full registered company name goes in, with its spaces turned into hyphens and the word that says what kind of company it is left out, because the sub-domain already says that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo raises no issues relating to network security. It does add one requirement for registries: when delegating entries in sub-domains, the registries must ensure that the application contains sufficient evidence of the legal rights to a given name.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says nothing about network security. Its one rule for registries is that an applicant has to show evidence that it holds the legal right to the name it is asking for.
